Stage 3 · Language

Saying what you think, and how strongly

The same opinion, in four different strengths.

Read these four sentences from a discussion.
  • As far as I’m concerned, anything that makes people think is a good idea.
  • Don’t you think it would be better if people simply stopped buying?
  • I’m convinced that people would change if they understood the damage.
  • If you ask me, we have to give people a better option.
Which one asks the other person for their opinion instead of giving one?
An opinion stated bare sounds like a fact. English expects you to frame it.

This lesson is about functional language rather than a verb form, but the phrases work in a fixed way and have to be learnt as carefully as any tense. Their job is social: they mark a statement as your view rather than as objective truth, and they leave room for the other person to disagree without a confrontation.

Compare Guilt-free brands are pointless with If you ask me, guilt-free brands are pointless. The content is identical. The first sounds like an announcement of fact and invites an argument; the second signals that you know this is one opinion among several. In English-speaking professional and social settings, the second is not merely more polite — it is more persuasive, because it does not force the listener to defend their position before they have heard your reason.

There are four moves to control. Opening an opinion (In my opinion, / Personally, / If you ask me, / I’d say…); softening a strong claim so it can be discussed (probably, I’d say, it seems to me); asking for somebody else’s view (What do you think? What do you reckon? Don’t you think…?); and responding, which is graded from full agreement (I couldn’t agree more) through partial agreement (That’s a fair point, but…) to disagreement (I see what you mean, but…).

One grammatical point sits underneath all of this and is worth noticing now, because it recurs throughout the level: English attaches the negative to the opinion verb, not to the clause. Say I don’t think it’s fair, not I think it isn’t fair. The second is understandable but sounds blunt and non-native.

Before you look at the table: the tables below set out the phrases by position — front, middle or end of the sentence — and by strength. Position matters: most opinion openers go at the front and take a comma.
What to say, and how strong it sounds
What you are doingNeutralStrongerSofter / more careful
Giving an opinionIn my opinion… · I think…I’m convinced that… · As far as I’m concerned…I’d say… · It seems to me that…
Asking for oneWhat do you think?Don’t you think…?What do you reckon? · How do you feel about…?
AgreeingI agree.I couldn’t agree more.That’s a fair point.
DisagreeingI don’t agree.I’m afraid I disagree.I see what you mean, but… · I’m not so sure.

Almost all of these take a state verb recycled — think, agree, mean, seem, be convinced. So they stay in the simple form: I think you’re right, never I’m thinking you’re right.

Two register rules. What do you reckon? and If you ask me are spoken and informal — fine in a post or with friends, wrong in an email to a company. In my opinion and It seems to me that work everywhere.

Softening is not weakness. Starting a disagreement with I see what you mean, but… makes people listen. Starting with You’re wrong ends the conversation. At B1+ the softener is the skill, not the opinion.

Full grammar reference — the language of opinions — giving, softening and responding

What it is

This lesson is about functional language rather than a single verb form: the fixed phrases English uses to introduce an opinion, to make it sound less absolute, to ask for someone else’s, and to agree or disagree with it. These phrases behave like grammar — they have a fixed shape and a fixed position — so they have to be learnt whole.

What it means, and what it does

An opinion stated bare (Guilt-free brands are pointless) sounds like a fact and invites conflict. An opinion framed (If you ask me, guilt-free brands are pointless) signals that you know it is only your view. The frame does not change the content; it changes the social effect, and at B1 that difference is what separates a blunt speaker from a persuasive one.

When and why we use it

This lesson is about functional language rather than a verb form, but the phrases work in a fixed way and have to be learnt as carefully as any tense. Their job is social: they mark a statement as your view rather than as objective truth, and they leave room for the other person to disagree without a confrontation.

Compare Guilt-free brands are pointless with If you ask me, guilt-free brands are pointless. The content is identical. The first sounds like an announcement of fact and invites an argument; the second signals that you know this is one opinion among several. In English-speaking professional and social settings, the second is not merely more polite — it is more persuasive, because it does not force the listener to defend their position before they have heard your reason.

There are four moves to control. Opening an opinion (In my opinion, / Personally, / If you ask me, / I’d say…); softening a strong claim so it can be discussed (probably, I’d say, it seems to me); asking for somebody else’s view (What do you think? What do you reckon? Don’t you think…?); and responding, which is graded from full agreement (I couldn’t agree more) through partial agreement (That’s a fair point, but…) to disagreement (I see what you mean, but…).

One grammatical point sits underneath all of this and is worth noticing now, because it recurs throughout the level: English attaches the negative to the opinion verb, not to the clause. Say I don’t think it’s fair, not I think it isn’t fair. The second is understandable but sounds blunt and non-native.

Typical situations

You need this language whenever you take part in a discussion, comment on something online, react to news, review a product or a film, or take a side in a debate. It is also the backbone of the written opinion post you will produce in this lesson.

  • Introducing your own view — the phrase goes at the front of the sentence, followed by a comma in writing.In my opinion, we buy far more than we need.
  • Softening a strong claim — hedging words make a claim easier to disagree with politely.I’d say it’s probably more about image than quality.
  • Asking for someone’s view — a direct question, or a tag that invites a reply.What do you reckon? · Don’t you think it’s expensive?
  • Agreeing — strength matters: I couldn’t agree more is far stronger than I suppose so.I couldn’t agree more. · That’s a fair point.
  • Disagreeing politely — acknowledge first, then object — the two-part move.I see what you mean, but the price is the real problem.
  • Writing it for social media — the same functions, compressed: a claim, a reason, and a question to the reader.In my opinion that isn’t a problem — it’s the point. What do you reckon?

How it differs from similar structures

I don’t agree (direct, can sound sharp) · I’m not sure I agree (softened) · I see what you mean, but… (softened and constructive). At B1, prefer the last two with people you do not know well.
What do you think? (neutral, works everywhere) · What do you reckon? (informal, friends and social media) · What’s your view on…? (formal, meetings and writing).

How to build it

Opening an opinion: In my opinion, / If you ask me, / Personally, / As far as I’m concerned, + clause
Hedged opinion: I’d say (that) + clause  ·  I think + clause
Asking: What do you think / reckon (about…)?  ·  Don’t you think (that) + clause?
Agreeing / disagreeing: I couldn’t agree more.  ·  I see what you mean, but + clause
Front positionIn my opinion, the price is too high. — comma after the phrase.
Mid or end positionThe price is too high, if you ask me. — also natural, slightly softer.
Negative opinionSay I don’t think it’s fair, not I think it isn’t fair.
Question formDo you think it’s worth it? · What do you reckon?
Responding — agreeingAbsolutely. · That’s a fair point. · I couldn’t agree more.
Responding — disagreeingI see your point, but… · I’m not so sure. · I’d have to disagree.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • English prefers negative raising: the negative attaches to the opinion verb, not to the clause. I don’t think he’s right is standard; I think he isn’t right sounds blunt or odd.
  • I couldn’t agree more means total agreement, not disagreement. The negative is what makes it strong: there is no more agreement available.
  • Reckon is informal and conversational. Use it in speech and social posts, not in an essay or a professional email.
  • Personally and As far as I’m concerned both mark a view as yours alone, but the second is heavier and often introduces disagreement.
  • In writing, an opinion phrase is followed by a comma. Missing it is one of the most visible errors in B1 written work.
  • Do not stack two openers: In my opinion, I think that… says the same thing twice. Choose one.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • In my opinion I think we buy too much. → In my opinion, we buy too much.One opinion frame is enough, and it takes a comma.
  • According to me, it is a waste. → In my opinion, it is a waste.According to reports somebody else’s view, never your own.
  • I am agree with you. → I agree with you.Agree is a full verb in English; it takes no be.
  • I think it isn’t worth it. → I don’t think it’s worth it.English moves the negative onto think.
  • I couldn’t agree more with you, I disagree. → I couldn’t agree more.I couldn’t agree more already means full agreement.
  • What you think about it? → What do you think about it?A wh- question still needs the auxiliary do.

More examples in context

  • statingIn my opinion, we don’t choose phones any more — we’re told when to want one.
  • softeningI’d say it’s more about image than quality.
  • personalPersonally, I’d rather repair something than replace it.
  • informal askSo what do you reckon — worth it or not?
  • inviting a replyDon’t you think the price is the real issue?
  • strong agreementI couldn’t agree more. That’s exactly what happened to me.
  • partial agreementThat’s a fair point, but not everyone can afford to pay more.
  • polite disagreementI see what you mean, but the companies aren’t the whole story.
  • hedged claimIt’s probably the most expensive way to feel better.
  • closing a postThat’s the bit nobody puts in a caption. What do you reckon?

A tip for remembering it

Build every opinion as three moves: frame → claim → reason. If you ask me (frame), a new phone every two years is unnecessary (claim), because the old one still works (reason). When you reply to someone, add a fourth move first: acknowledge what they said before you object.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Frame an opinion instead of stating it bare: In my opinion, / If you ask me, / I’d say…
  2. Put the frame at the front and follow it with a comma.
  3. Move the negative onto the opinion verb: I don’t think it’s fair.
  4. I agree takes no be; I couldn’t agree more means you agree completely.
  5. Disagree in two parts: acknowledge, then object — I see what you mean, but…
  6. Match the register: reckon for friends, What’s your view? for work.

What the model does, in four moves
  • One concrete detail first — not a general statement.
  • The opinion, marked — so nobody has to guess which part is your view.
  • One reason, and only one. A post is not an essay.
  • A question back, so the thread can continue.
  • Then write your own three-post thread on a topic you care about: a concrete detail, your opinion clearly marked, one reason, and a question back.

2 · Take a side. Work in pairs.
Student A — for

Guilt-free brands are real progress. Argue for them. Use one strong phrase (I’m convinced…) and one softener (That’s a fair point, but…).

Student B — against

They are just a more expensive way to feel better. Argue against. Use I see what you mean, but… at least once, and ask A a question.

Then swap sides and run it again. The second run is where the phrases get learned.

2 · Take a side. Your teacher takes the other one.
You — choose your side

Guilt-free brands: real progress, or an expensive excuse? Choose, and argue it. Use one strong phrase and one softener.

Your teacher — the other side

Argues against you and asks one hard question.

Then swap sides and argue the opposite. Two minutes each.

2 · Take both sides out loud.

One minute for guilt-free brands, one minute against. Use a different opening phrase every time you start a new point.

3 · Now write your own thread. Three posts, 120–180 words in total.
Your plan
  • Post 1 — one concrete detail, then your opinion, marked, then one reason. Finish with a hashtag.
  • Post 2 — somebody disagrees. Write their reply, starting with a softener.
  • Post 3 — you answer. Give ground once (That’s a fair point), add one new idea, and end with a question to your readers.
